│ rules [add|rm]               │ stored approval rules                                │
╰──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Key Default Meaning tools true Offer tools at all. tools_policy allowlist allowlist, ask or auto (see approvals). tools_shell_allow [] Extra commands for the shell allowlist. tools_timeout 120 Per-tool subprocess timeout, seconds. tools_max_output 4000 Chars of tool output that go back to the model. tools_max_rounds 8 Tool rounds per turn before the loop stops. tool_colors {} Per-tool panel colours, e.g. {"run_shell": "green"}.

--tools/--no-tools override for a run; /tools on|off for a session, and /tools NAME on|off per tool. Disabled tools are not sent to the model at all, so it does not waste a round calling something that cannot run.

docs.title: The record
docs.text: Calls, results and approvals are stored on the session like any other message, so --show replays them the way they looked live, and exports include them. A tool loop that ends in an answer is separated from it by a centered response divider; a round that is still working keeps the plain rule.

docs.title: Where the pieces live
docs.text:
• Definitions (what the model sees): ollamarun_lib/defs/tools/*.json, overridable per user — Definitions.
  • Approval policy: the allowlist, rules engine and dangerous_command floor — Approvals and policy.
  • The loop: runtime.py drives rounds; repl.py renders them — Architecture.

docs.title: Approvals and policy
docs.text: Nothing the model asks for runs just because it asked. Every call is classified, and only the clearly safe classes go unattended.

docs.title: What runs unattended
docs.text:
Class Examples Why Read-only tools read_file, list_dir, fetch_url, web_search, search_sessions, list_models, system_status, context_status, session_info read_only: true in the definition; nothing is modified. speak — always_safe: true (speaking changes nothing). Safe-listed shell ls, cat, grep, rg, find, wc, file, stat, tree, du, df, sort, cut, tr, diff, echo, date, which, whoami, uname, read-only git Every segment of the pipeline is on the list, with no substitutions, redirections or grouping. Provably harmless Python print(6*7) Only safe modules/nodes; no filesystem, network, imports of os/sys, calls like open/eval. Rule-covered calls a remembered exact call, a shell:/path:/python: rule You granted it earlier this session. Policy auto, or -y/--yes — Everything runs; the sharpest tool in the box.

Everything else asks in the REPL and is denied with a note in an unattended run.

docs.title: The ask
docs.text:
The prompt lists numbered choices — run once, remember exactly this call, one line per suggested generalized rule, auto-allow, deny:

write_file needs confirmation: write_file modifies state
  1/y  run once
  2/a  always allow exactly this call
  3    always allow path: /tmp/script-check.txt (this session)
  4/A  auto-allow every later call  [CAREFUL]
  5/n  deny
choose (1): 1

Type a number or the letter; Enter takes option 1. Choosing a rule prints a allowed by rule … note on later calls it covers.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
A rule is a session-scoped grant, stored in the session under tool_rules (and tool_allow for exact remembered calls). Four kinds:

Kind Covers Label call exactly one call, by fingerprint exactly this call shell one command's literal prefix; an implicit :* tail shell: mkdir -p :* path one tool's path argument, by glob relative to the directory it ran in path: ~/proj/** python a run_python snippet importing/using only the listed module roots python: imports math, statistics

/tools rules lists them; /tools rules add KIND PATTERN stores one by hand and /tools rules rm N removes it. Suggestions are built from the call being approved (suggest_rules in tools.py), so the number of choices varies — a compound shell command, for example, only ever offers the exact-call grant.

docs.title: The floor no rule covers
docs.text:
dangerous_command() is the set of things a shell rule may never soften; they prompt again every time, even under a stored rule:

  • variable or backtick substitution ($…, `…`),
  • output/input redirection (>, <) and grouping/brace expansion ((), {}),
  • pipes into an interpreter (curl … | sh, … | python3),
  • privilege/wrapper commands (sudo, doas, su, env, xargs, nice, nohup, timeout, …),
  • interpreters themselves (sh, bash, python, node, …),
  • disk/power/network level tools (dd, mkfs, mount, shutdown, iptables, nc, …),
  • a recursive rm aimed at a whole root (/, ~, *, ., …).

The same floor keeps unsafe Python out: open, exec, eval, os, sys, subprocess, socket, network/OS modules and friends always prompt.

docs.title: Shell details
docs.text:
shell_safety() splits a command line on |, ||, &&, ;, & and newlines and checks every segment: each must be on the allowlist and free of the floor above. git is allowed only for read-only subcommands (status, log, diff, show, …; git config only through --get /--list-style flags). tools_shell_allow in the config adds commands of your own to the allowlist (remember: best-effort last).

Python's version splits a snippet into imports, calls and attribute access; its allowlist of modules (math, json, re, statistics, …) is what the safe list covers. Everything else asks.

docs.title: Unattended runs
docs.text:
A non-interactive run (piped output, no terminal) cannot ask, so an otherwise-askable call is denied as a result:

╭─ tool · write_file · failed ─────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ $ /tmp/unattended-demo.txt (5 chars)                                         │
│ tool not run: not auto-approved (write_file modifies state) and this run is  │
│ unattended                                                                   │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

The model sees that and reacts. -y/--yes makes everything run (verified: the same call writes the file and the answer arrives); /tools policy auto does the same for a session. --tools / --no-tools switch the harness off entirely for a run.

docs.title: Policy modes and configuration
docs.text: Key / command Effect /tools policy auto\|allowlist\|ask Global mode. ask asks for everything not always-safe; allowlist is the default; auto approves everything. --yes / -y Per-run auto approval (also silences --delete). tools_policy, tools_shell_allow, tools_timeout, tools_max_output, tools_max_rounds Config defaults for the above. See Tools. /tools NAME on\|off, /tools enable\|disable NAME… Take tools out of the model's menu.

docs.title: Over the API
docs.text: The agent API runs the same engine, but its policy is never auto: sessions submit with approval: "interactive" to park undecided calls for a client decision, or approval: "policy" to let the allowlist/rules decide and deny the rest with a note.

docs.title: Tool definitions
docs.text: What the model sees of a tool — its name, description and JSON-schema parameters — is data, not code. One JSON file per tool under ollamarun_lib/defs/tools/, and a same-named file in ~/etc/config_files/ollamarun-defs/tools/ overrides it.

docs.title: The format
docs.text:
read_file.json, shipped verbatim:

{
  "name": "read_file",
  "description": "Read a text file (optionally a line range) from the local machine.",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "path": {"type": "string", "description": "file path"},
      "offset": {"type": "integer", "description": "first line (0-based)"},
      "limit": {"type": "integer", "description": "how many lines"}
    },
    "required": ["path"]
  },
  "handler": "read_file",
  "read_only": true
}
Field Required Meaning name yes The tool's name; must match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*. description yes Model-facing text — say what it does and when to use it; this is the model's only documentation. parameters yes JSON schema with type: "object", properties, optional required. handler yes The Python handler name, looked up in tools.py's HANDLERS. read_only no true = never asks; the calls are read-only by construction. always_safe no true = never asks even though it does something (used by speak). requires no A capability gate; the tool only appears when it resolves. aliases no Invented names that resolve onto this tool.

parameters may be an empty object ("properties": {}, "required": []); the schema is what build_tool_schemas() hands to Ollama, so valid JSON-schema shapes work as they do anywhere.

docs.title: Capability gates
docs.text:
requires The tool appears when Uninstalled tool's help says search ddgs is importable the ddgs package (pip install ddgs) tts a tts-remote command resolves the tts-remote command chem a chemInventoryAPI command resolves the chemInventoryAPI command (config: chem_inventory) artifacts a serve artifact store is injected the serve artifact store (ollamarun serve)

/tools NAME help still works for an uninstalled tool — it shows the definition and what it needs.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text: aliases maps the names models invent onto the real tool: search → web_search, curl → fetch_url, mkdir → make_dir, recall → search_sessions, and so on. Call-id-prefixed names (call_fetch_url) are also resolved by stripping the prefix and retrying. Aliases show up in /tools NAME help and complete in the REPL.

docs.title: Overrides
docs.text:
Put a same-named file in ~/etc/config_files/ollamarun-defs/tools/ and it replaces the shipped one (same name, whole definition). That is how you reword a tool for your own models, tighten a schema or add aliases without touching Python. Worked example — an override whose description starts with CUSTOM OVERRIDE::

$ mkdir -p ~/etc/config_files/ollamarun-defs/tools
$ cat > ~/etc/config_files/ollamarun-defs/tools/read_file.json <<'EOF'
{
  "name": "read_file",
  "description": "CUSTOM OVERRIDE: read a text file. Prefer this over run_shell cat.",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "path": {"type": "string", "description": "file path"},
      "offset": {"type": "integer", "description": "first line (0-based)"},
      "limit": {"type": "integer", "description": "how many lines"}
    },
    "required": ["path"]
  },
  "handler": "read_file",
  "read_only": true
}
EOF

Next session, the change is live:

llama3.2:3b › /tools read_file help
read_file — on
CUSTOM OVERRIDE: read a text file. Prefer this over run_shell cat.
model calls it with read_file(path, offset?, limit?)
…

A broken file never breaks the harness — it warns and is skipped, and the shipped definition stays in effect:

ignoring tool definition ~/etc/config_files/ollamarun-defs/tools/broken.json:
bad JSON: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 3 (char 2)

The loader reads the shipped directory first, then the override directory, so a later layer wins per file stem (load_tool_definitions()); duplicate tool names inside one load are also skipped with a warning.

docs.title: A truly new tool
docs.text: Overriding only changes what exists: the handler must still be a function tools.py knows. Adding a new capability is therefore two steps — a JSON file plus the handler function and its HANDLERS entry in ollamarun_lib/tools.py — and the loader picks the file up automatically. The handlers page in Contributing is the short version.

docs.title: The sibling: prompts
docs.text: Tool wording is model-facing text; the system/title/summarize prompts are the other half of it, with the same override-directory mechanism — see Prompts.

docs.title: Running tools yourself
docs.text:
/tools NAME call ARGS runs a tool exactly like the model would — same approval gate, same panels — without adding anything to the conversation. Three argument forms:

  • JSON: /tools read_file call {"path": "/etc/hostname"}
  • keyed pairs: /tools run_shell call command="echo hi"
  • one bare value, only when exactly one parameter is required: /tools run_python call print(6*7)

That last rule has a sharp edge: list_dir's path is optional, so /tools list_dir call /tmp refuses with a usage line — use /tools list_dir call path=/tmp.

docs.title: The tool loop
docs.text: A turn with tools is a loop of rounds. Each round is one /api/chat request; between rounds the harness runs whatever the model asked for and feeds the results back.

docs.title: One round, step by step
docs.text:
1. Request out. The payload carries the enabled tool schemas (build_chat_payload in client.py), so the model can choose to call one instead of answering.
  2. Call in. When the reply contains tool_calls, each one is printed as a coloured call panel with its arguments (pretty-printed JSON).
  3. Decision. The call goes through the approval gate: auto, safe-listed, rule-covered, or asking you — a denied call is a normal result, not an error.
  4. Execution. The handler runs (bash -lc for run_shell, a short Python program for run_python, direct file I/O for the file tools).
  5. Result out. The result panel prints below the call panel, wearing the same colour, with ok/failed and the duration in its title.
  6. Next round. The call and its result are appended to the session as an assistant message with tool_calls plus one tool message per result, and the model is asked again — now with the results in context.
  7. Done. A reply with no tool calls ends the turn. After a tool loop the final answer is separated from the working rounds by a centered response divider.

Rounds are capped by tools_max_rounds (default 8). Past the cap the loop warns and appends not executed: tool-call limit reached results so the model still knows why nothing ran.

docs.title: A real loop
docs.text:
Here is a genuine (if over-eager) round — the model was told "say hello" and decided a shell command was the way to do it:

llama3.2:3b ›
╭─ tool · run_shell ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ {                                                                            │
│   "command": "echo Hello!"                                                   │
│ }                                                                            │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
running run_shell…
╭─ tool · run_shell · ok · 0.00s ──────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ $ echo Hello!                                                                │
│ exit 0                                                                       │
│ Hello!                                                                       │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
llama3.2:3b ›
How can I help you today?

Round 1 asked for run_shell; echo is on the safe list so it ran unattended; round 2 answered. The result panel tells the whole story: the command, its exit code and its output.

docs.title: When the call needs approval
docs.text:
This one modified state, so the harness stopped and asked (condensed):

llama3.2:3b › Use write_file to write the text hello-from-the-model to /tmp/script-check.txt.
╭─ tool · write_file ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ { "append": false, "content": "hello-from-the-model",                        │
│   "path": "/tmp/script-check.txt" }                                          │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
running write_file…
write_file needs confirmation: write_file modifies state
  1/y  run once
  2/a  always allow exactly this call
  3    always allow path: /tmp/script-check.txt (this session)
  4/A  auto-allow every later call  [CAREFUL]
  5/n  deny
choose (1): 1
╭─ tool · write_file · ok · 0.00s ─────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ $ /tmp/script-check.txt (20 chars)                                           │
│ wrote 20 chars to /tmp/script-check.txt                                      │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
llama3.2:3b ›
The written text is indeed "hello-from-the-model" and its length is 20 characters.

The choices are numbered and typed; y/a/A/n are accepted as the letters for run / remember / auto / deny. Option 3 was a suggested generalized rule for that path, stored in the session. The gate is covered in Approvals and policy.

docs.title: Failures are results
docs.text:
A tool failure does not break the turn — it becomes text the model reads. Here is an unattended one-shot trying to write a file without -y:

╭─ tool · write_file · failed ─────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ $ /tmp/unattended-demo.txt (5 chars)                                         │
│ tool not run: not auto-approved (write_file modifies state) and this run is  │
│ unattended                                                                   │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

The model now knows the write did not happen and can try something else, explain, or ask. With -y the same call runs (verified: the file is written and the answer says done).

docs.title: What the model actually receives
docs.text:
• Each result's text is what the handler produced — stdout and exit status for run_shell, the program output for run_python, file content for read_file.
  • tools_max_output (default 4000 chars) caps what goes back; a cut is marked …[truncated: N of M chars omitted]…. The panel may show fewer lines than the model got (… N more lines (full output sent to the model)), so a long listing never floods your terminal.
  • tools_timeout (default 120 s) bounds a subprocess; a timeout is reported like any other failure.

docs.title: Cancelling a turn
docs.text: Ctrl+C stops the current turn. Subprocess-backed tools are killed by process group (through run_cancellable()), network tools are abandoned rather than waited on, and a destructive call that arrives after the stop is refused instead of run. Whatever completed before the cancel stays in the session.

docs.title: Prompts
docs.text:
The model-facing text lives in files, not code:

  • ollamarun_lib/defs/prompts/ — system.md (the built-in default system prompt), system_tools.md (the tool, web-search, math-in-code and tool-result rules, appended when tools are on), title.md and summarize.md (both take the text to wrap as {{content}}).

A same-named file under ~/etc/config_files/ollamarun-defs/prompts/ overrides the shipped one, so prompts can be tuned without touching Python.

Every request carries a system prompt: the session's own (--system, --system-file, config system, /system TEXT) when set, the built-in default otherwise. --no-system / config system: "" / /system off send none, /system clear returns to the default, and /system alone shows what is in effect. It is sent as a leading system message and never enters the saved history.

Tool wording is the other half of the model-facing text — see Tool definitions.

docs.title: API layer
docs.text:
Evolve ollamarun from a CLI-oriented agent harness into a reusable agent backend: an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API plus native endpoints for agent-specific functionality, all on one agent runtime. The per-phase plans in plans/ are the source of truth; this file is only the itemized index.

The layer landed across Phases 1–10 (all rows below are done); v2.0 is the milestone release that marks the surface as the supported, tested contract.

docs.title: Design principles (locked)
docs.text:
• OpenAI-compatible at heart. Familiar request/response schemas, endpoints, streaming semantics and error formats; the same style for extensions.
  • Extend without breaking compatibility. Agent-specific features never require nonstandard fields in ordinary OpenAI-compatible requests.
  • Reuse the existing runtime. No duplicated agent loop, tool implementations, approval logic or session handling in HTTP layers.
  • Keep the backend lean. Existing dependencies and the standard library; no heavyweight web framework without a concrete need.
  • Structured events internally. Responses, tools, approvals, artifacts, errors and cancellation have explicit representations.
  • Secure by default. The API is LAN-accessible without authentication (locked): default 0.0.0.0:11440, --bind to narrow it, trusted-network only, never exposed to the public internet. Tool policy is preserved exactly — network access is never authorization.

docs.title: Locked decisions (cross-phase)
docs.text:
• LAN-accessible without authentication. 0.0.0.0:11440 by default, --bind IP [--port N] to change it; the API listener stays separate from Ollama's --host. The service is trusted-network-only and must never be exposed directly to the public internet. Authentication, when added later, wraps the routes without reshaping them and is never a substitute for tool approval.
  • Two streaming contracts, one runtime. /v1/chat/completions speaks OpenAI SSE only; the typed turn.* event stream (seq, replay, stream.gap) belongs to the native agent endpoints and never leaks onto the OpenAI wire.
  • Model turns and agent turns stay distinguishable. A model turn is one inference call: client tools pass through and come back as tool_calls, never executed. An agent turn runs the internal tool loop.
  • Disconnect policy. A model-only completion may cancel upstream generation on disconnect; a native agent turn keeps running — a disconnect is an unsubscribe and cancellation stays an explicit operation.
  • Turns are in-memory; the session JSON is the durable record. A server restart destroys live turn records; expired/missing turns are recovered from the session store. GET /v1/agent/turns/{id} answers 404 (never existed) and 410 (deliberately swept) distinctly.
  • One active turn per session inside the process; the initial contract is single-writer (CLI and API never mutate one persistent session at the same time). Cross-process session locking is a later upgrade.
  • Approvals are explicit state: every pending approval has its own id tied to one turn and one tool operation, the first resolution wins, a timeout defaults to denial, and cancellation/shutdown resolve waiting approvals as cancelled.
  • Context fitting and placement control are native-surface features. The OpenAI-compatible surface stays a stateless translation proxy and never gains num_ctx/gpu_layers fields (one request is one inference call; there is no session to configure and fitting per request would mean load churn per completion).

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• ollamarun runs as a reusable backend without terminal interaction; the CLI keeps using the same runtime.
  • Standard OpenAI clients do chat completions (streaming included) against a custom base URL; unsupported features fail explicitly and are documented.
  • Native endpoints expose full agent turns, sessions, approvals and artifacts with the lifecycle properties above.
  • Tool policies and security controls stay enforced independently of the client; automated compatibility and regression tests cover the critical paths; a separate web UI can be built entirely as a client.

Out of scope for this stage: building the web UI, redesigning the reasoning loop, distributed orchestration, replacing existing tool implementations.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
ollamarun_lib/ is organized as pipeline stages, one module per stage; read a module's own docstring for what lives there before editing:

  1. constants.py — shared stdlib/rich/optional-dependency imports, VERSION, config/session/log paths, THEME, the shared console singleton, DEFAULT_CONFIG, the DEFAULT_SERVE_* transport/limit defaults, and the tool-panel colours (TOOL_COLORS/ TOOL_COLOR_PALETTE, tool_color() with its random per-run fallback, set_tool_colors() for the config tool_colors overrides). Every other module sits on top of this one.
  2. helpers.py — small helpers: ISO timestamps, id generation, bool/host/think coercion, --remote resolution (resolve_remote, remote_node, tailscale_map, tailscale_peer_state, is_local_host), disk-space probes (local_free_disk, ssh_free_disk — the ssh probes take a cancel token), run_cancellable()/CommandCancelled (the process-group-killing subprocess runner every tool shares), config load (load_config) and the response-timings policy (resolve_show_stats), logging setup, and the count formatters shared by both front ends (human_tokens/format_context for the ctx counter, human_chars, human_duration), serve_settings() (the one validated serve_* policy matrix: defaults, types, ranges and zero semantics, consumed by serve_main), model_allowed() (the serve_models tag-aware fnmatch allowlist) and ModelTracker (the models a serve process used, for unload-on-exit).
  3. mathrender.py — LaTeX → Unicode, combined in one module because the two halves call into each other: regex-level conversion for inline math (convert_math, latex_to_unicode) falls through to the 2D layout engine's render_inline_math for inline math, and the layout engine falls back to convert_math/latex_to_unicode for anything unsupported. The layout engine is a self-contained parser/box-layout system for display math ($$...$$, \[...\]): _tokenize_math → _MathParser → an AST of M* node classes (MFrac, MSqrt, MScript, MBigOp, MMatrix, MCases, MAligned, MBoxed, etc.) → _layout() builds a _Box (list-of-strings + width) recursively → _flatten() is the plain-text fallback path. render_display_math()/render_inline_math() are the public entry points; both must never raise — anything unsupported (unknown environment, over-wide, over-budget) falls through to pylatexenc. This module also has render_content()/render_thinking() (markdown + centered display math, used by the renderer and REPL). Changes here need care: the layout is hand-rolled string-grid arithmetic, not a real typesetting library.
  4. files.py — @file mentions: expand_file_mentions() inlines file contents into a prompt.
  5. images.py — encode_image/image_payload, base64 embedding with max_file_kb truncation.
  6. renderer.py — Renderer class drives a rich.Live view: incremental markdown re-render while tokens stream, the collapsible thinking panel (render_thinking, Ctrl+T expand/collapse in place; /thinking full prints the stored panel directly), and TpsEstimator (windowed()/average()/rate()) for the live footer: windowed rate, cumulative average, streamed tokens and a ctx counter that counts the round's chunks on top of the context_used/ context_total the REPL passes in, and the per-response ⏱ timings line whose visibility comes from resolve_show_stats() (on by default on a terminal, piped output only with --verbose, config show_stats: false as the off-switch). StreamSink is the seam the TUI uses: with a sink, stream() pushes the same frames to a widget instead of a rich.Live, so both front ends share one streaming loop (and stream(cancel=…) honors a CancelToken). Also has the chat-bubble helpers (user_message_box, small right-aligned box for a user turn; model_message_panel, full-width titled box for a model turn) and the tool panels -- tool_call_panel()/tool_result_panel(), both coloured by constants.tool_color() so every tool keeps one identity across the live view and the transcript (tool_result_panel also takes a note that lands in the title -- the speak tool's optiplex → g3, persisted on the tool message as tool_note) -- plus render_transcript() (replays a saved session the way it looked live, used by /show/--show). This is the piece that talks to the terminal frame-by-frame; changes to streaming UX go here. consume_chunk() is the shared per-chunk accumulator and HeadlessRenderer is the terminal-free presenter (it emits message.delta events instead of printing), used by the runtime's headless turns.
  7. client.py — OllamaClient wraps /api/chat, /api/generate, /api/embed, /api/ps, /api/pull, /api/create etc. over raw requests, streaming response bodies line-by-line (including pull progress events). build_chat_payload() assembles the request body from CLI args + session history.
  8. tools.py — the tool harness: ToolSpec/default_registry() (shell, python, files — read/write/list plus edit_file and the make_dir/move_file/copy_file/delete_file chores — web_search when ddgs is installed, fetch_url, search_sessions, list_models, system_status, context_status/session_info, tts-remote speak/list_voices, and the chemInventoryAPI lookup tools when that CLI is present), the allowlist policy (shell_safety, python_safety, approval_decision), the approval-rule engine (ToolRule, suggest_rules, rule_matches, dangerous_command), argument normalization, output truncation and execute_tool(). The tool declarations load from the definition files — one JSON per tool under defs/tools/ (ToolDefinition, load_tool_definitions(); HANDLERS maps the JSON's handler name onto the function, requires gates a tool on a capability, tool_aliases() is built from the aliases lists so invented names like search/curl resolve onto the real tools, and resolve_tool_alias() strips a call-id prefix (call_fetch_url) and retries on a miss; bad files warn and are skipped). ToolSpec keeps each definition's requires and aliases (REQUIREMENT_HINTS words them for the help pages). ToolHandlerResult(text, artifact_paths) is the optional structured handler return: execute_tool() registers regular files through ToolContext.artifacts (the turn-bound TurnArtifacts publisher the serve API injects) and attaches the refs to the ToolOutcome; plain strings still work for every handler that produces no files. ToolContext carries the runtime seams the REPL injects: client/store (list_models, system_status, search_sessions), ssh_target/ssh_user for remote probes, chem_inventory (the CLI path override), artifacts (the serve publisher), context_report/session_report (the plain dicts Repl.context_report()/session_report() assemble for the awareness tools) and workspace (the API path jail: when set, path arguments and the run_shell/run_python working directories resolve under it and resolved escapes including symlinks are refused; the CLI leaves it unset). The web half is self-contained: _HTMLTextExtractor/extract_html_text turn pages into readable text plus links, extract_pdf_text uses pypdf or pdftotext, format_fetch_response maps a response onto model-readable text (never the site's error page), run_web_search wraps ddgs. The speech half speaks through run_tts_say() (an older tts-remote without --json is retried without it) and turns the say --json plan into the shared title_note via speech_hosts(). The agent loop that calls into it lives in runtime.py (approve → execute → append a role: tool message → ask the model again), auto-speak lives in Repl.speak_text, and rendering of calls/results is renderer.py. ToolContext.cancel reaches every subprocess-backed tool (shell, python, the ssh probes, chemInventoryAPI, tts-remote, trash-put) through helpers.run_cancellable(), and ToolRunner abandons network tools (fetch_url, web_search) on cancel so the result is discarded instead of waited on.
  9. prompts.py — the prompt files: load_prompt() (override layer first, shipped default after, cached per process; missing/unreadable warns and reads as None), default_system_prompt() (composes system.md + system_tools.md when tools are on), title_prompt()/summarize_prompt() (both expand {{content}}) and render_prompt(). Defaults live in defs/prompts/.
  10. events.py — the runtime event vocabulary: RuntimeEvent plus the turn.*/message.*/tool.*/approval.* type constants, artifact.created and session.fit, and TERMINAL_EVENTS. A leaf module (no imports from the package) shared by renderer.py, runtime.py and the HTTP layer; envelopes, sequence numbers and replay are added on top of the same types, so nothing here depends on transport.
  11. session.py — Session (in-memory conversation model: messages, model, system prompt, options; artifacts accumulates the refs the conversation saw, add_artifacts() dedupes by id) and SessionStore (atomic read/write of the JSON files + index.json, list/search/export/delete; its index read-modify-write runs under a shared RLock plus an exclusive flock on <index>.lock (so a CLI saving while serve runs cannot lose entries) and its temp files are named per writer. export_markdown/export_json/export_html are the three export formats.
  12. emit.py — emit() plus the cli_list/cli_search/cli_show/ cli_export/cli_delete functions that implement the non-interactive inspection flags.
  13. ui.py — the front-end seam: Ui (the interactive hooks repl.py and interactive.py call: ask, confirm, editor, approval, notify, and interactive — whether the front end can actually ask), ConsoleUi (the inline implementation — the same rich prompts as always, notifications are a no-op; interactive follows console.is_terminal), the tool-approval choice list (approval_entries/approval_lines) and the numbered typed prompt _prompt_approval (moved here so the console prompt and the TUI modal are built from one list), and the status-bar model (StatusSnapshot, format_status(), spinner_frame()): plain data plus a pure formatter (context text via format_context, tps + tps_avg), unit-testable without a terminal.
  14. interactive.py — open_in_editor ($OLLAMA_EDITOR), pick_model/pick_session (fuzzy pickers; ui= routes the question to the TUI front end), model_context_length (reads context window from /api/show), and the missing-model flow: ensure_model() (free-space line + y/N pull prompt, --pull skip, picker on decline), pull_with_progress() and disk_free_line(). Model-list sorting lives here too: MODEL_SORT_KEYS/parse_model_sort (modified|name|size|parameters|context, plus aliases), model_parameter_count (parses details.parameter_size, MoE totals included), sort_models/model_table (shared by the picker and /model --list) and fetch_context_lengths/cached_context_length (one /api/show per uncached model, in parallel behind a status line, cached per host); pick_model takes sort=/on_sort= and its prompt accepts --sort KEY/-s KEY/sort KEY to re-order the table in place. Also the GPU-layer spec logic: model_block_count(), parse_gpu_layers_spec(), resolve_gpu_layers(), gpu_layers_label().
  15. ctxfit.py — the context fits behind /num-ctx --max-gpu and /num-ctx --max-cpu N: kv_bytes_per_token() (llama.cpp's KV formula applied to /api/show's GGUF metadata, per-layer head_count_kv arrays included), machine_state_for()/probe_machine_gpu() (free VRAM plus the ollama unit env) and machine_ram_for()/probe_machine_ram() (available DRAM from /proc/meminfo), locally or over one ssh probe each; estimate_max_gpu_ctx() (weights from /api/tags, llama.cpp's fit margin, resident models' /api/ps VRAM credited back, pinned /gpu-layers); estimate_max_cpu_ctx() (the budget is MemAvailable plus the resident model's own host RAM -- a reload returns it -- and the host footprint is the weights plus per-token KV of the layers llama.cpp's fit leaves on the CPU, max_cpu_overhead_mb reserved); the /api/ps-verified probe_max_gpu_ctx()/probe_max_cpu_ctx() that solve each next candidate from the measured affine footprint line instead of bisecting, plus ModelProfile/model_profile() (the parameters/quantization cross-check, per-layer KV geometry with sliding windows and MLA, ssm.*/shortconv recurrent state and the embedding/output/block weight split behind every estimate) and CtxCalibrationStore (bounded, host/model/placement-scoped measured samples that calibrate later estimates and seed probe search; stale/incompatible data falls back to the profile) (FitRequest/GpuFit/CpuFit/ProbeResult), the rich reports and max_gpu_context()/max_cpu_context(), which the REPL command and the CLI --num-ctx max-gpu / --num-ctx --max-cpu N flags both call. The probes themselves live in helpers.py (local_gpu_probe, ssh_gpu_probe, local_ram_probe, ssh_ram_probe, host_is_self).
  16. runtime.py — the agent turn runtime: AgentRuntime (the loop and tool execution that used to live in Repl._generate/ Repl._execute_tool_calls), TurnSettings, TurnHooks (the host seam: payload builder, presenter, approver, event sink, boundary drain), ApprovalRequest/ApprovalDecision, TurnResult, and the shared build_payload()/context_report()/session_report() helpers. It never prints and never touches a terminal; the CLI supplies a rich presenter and keeps thin wrappers with the old signatures, while HeadlessRenderer + an event sink drive it with no terminal at all. The runtime owns the tool-support capability check (once per model, after turn.started, warned as a turn.warning), and quiet_tools is read live so /render raw mid-turn takes effect. Tool artifacts: the runtime emits one artifact.created per ref between the approval decision and tool.result (which references the ids), stores the refs on the tool session message and accumulates them onto TurnResult.artifacts.
  17. turns.py — the turn manager: TurnEvent envelopes (turn id, 1-based seq, ISO timestamp, deterministic id), TurnManager (a worker thread per turn, one active turn per session, a global cap, per-turn buffers, replay with stream.gap, TTL retention swept on every entry point (subscribe() included), cancellation, begin_shutdown() (refuse new submissions before the ordered cancel/join), shutdown, and synthesized error terminals that carry the stable INTERNAL_ERROR_MESSAGE while the raw crash text goes to the --debug log and stays on the internal TurnResult), TurnHandle/Subscription/ TurnSnapshot, and the typed errors (SessionBusy/TooManyTurns/ UnknownTurn/TurnExpired) the HTTP layer maps to 409/429/404/410. It imports no front end: a host closure runs the runtime and returns a TurnResult; wait() joins a worker for tests and shutdown, and a subscriber that falls behind is closed, never stalling the turn.
  18. repl.py — SlashCompleter/completion_candidates (completion for /commands, session ids, models, @files, shared with the TUI input), the Repl class (the CLI adapter over runtime.AgentRuntime: _generate and _execute_tool_calls are thin wrappers that build the per-turn TurnHooks and render its events, _approve_tool_call is the policy + prompt approver, and the MessageQueue/CancelToken machinery is unchanged). headless + event_sink make the same object drivable with no terminal. _payload() is the one chat- request builder: it prepends the effective system prompt as a leading role: system message — Repl.effective_system() returns the session's text when set, the built-in default otherwise, None when disabled (empty string) — deliberately not stored in session.messages, so /system changes land on the next request and exports keep the history clean. Repl.context_length() is the one effective-window resolver behind the footer/status-bar ctx counter, /context and the 80%/85% warnings: a session num_ctx first, then the loaded runner's /api/ps context_length, then /api/show's model default; a show-only answer stays provisional until /api/ps reports the runner. model_show() is the run-long /api/show cache the length/block-count/awareness readers share, and context_report()/session_report() assemble the plain dicts the context_status/session_info tools format (window + usage, identity + settings + tool round). /system semantics live in _apply_system (clear/default → built-in, off → disabled, text → custom) plus _show_system, shared with /set system. Then the cmd_* functions. The numbered tool-approval prompt itself and the entry list it is built from (approval_entries/_prompt_approval, storing generalized ToolRules in the session) now live in ui.py, re-exported here so _prompt_approval keeps resolving from this module. Each slash command (/model//models, /set, /show, /load, /save, /pull, /num-ctx, /gpu-layers, /params, /tools, /tts, /think, /thinking, /system, /undo, /retry, /edit, /branch, /context, /summarize, /image, /render, /math, /pager, /tps, /copy, /export, /stats, /queue, ...) is a standalone cmd_NAME(repl, argument) function dispatched by name through COMMAND_HANDLERS; COMMAND_INFO is the authoritative description table (the REPL /help, the README's command table and the cli.py epilog all mirror it). Add a new slash command by adding one function here and wiring it into COMMAND_INFO/COMMAND_HANDLERS (and the hand-maintained build_parser() epilog in cli.py). /tools takes a tool name (or alias) as its first token for per-tool control — NAME on|off|help|call ARGS: _find_tool resolves aliases and falls back to tool_definitions() so an uninstalled tool still gets a page, _print_tool_help renders state/description/parameters/approval from the definition JSON, and _cmd_tools_call runs the tool through the normal approval gate without touching the conversation. completion_candidates/_tools_completion Tab-complete the whole command (subcommands, names and aliases, per-tool actions, policy modes, rule kinds) in both front ends. ps_table()/resolve_num_ctx() also live here since cmd_ps/ cmd_num_ctx are their only callers (resolve_num_ctx is reused by main() in cli.py for --num-ctx). ApprovalPicker and its runners are re-exported from ui.py for compatibility.
  19. tui.py — the optional Textual front end (--ui tui), deprecated: it will be rewritten as a pure ollamarun serve API client instead of reaching into the runtime in-process. Current code: the app (transcript pane / rule / status bar / always-on PromptInput), TuiStreamSink (the StreamSink that paints the streaming answer), TranscriptWriter (a file-like sink capturing everything printed through the shared console into the transcript), the modal screens (confirm, ask, and tool approval offering the same numbered choices as the console prompt) and TuiUi (the Ui implementation repl.py talks to). Turns and commands run in thread workers that marshal widget updates back with call_from_thread; run_tui() is the entry point. Textual is optional — cli.py's wants_tui() checks it and falls back to the inline REPL with a note.
  20. run.py — run_once() (non-REPL path, built on an already-constructed Repl; its --json branch runs the tool loop through AgentRuntime directly) and run_embed() (routes embedding-capable models to /api/embed instead of chat).
  21. server.py — the generic HTTP plumbing behind ollamarun serve: Router (method + {param} path patterns, with distinct 404/405), the Request/Response/StreamResponse model, HttpServer (a ThreadingHTTPServer wrapper with a body cap checked before the body is read — Content-Length and chunked alike, the chunked decoder enforcing the cumulative decoded cap before each chunk and rejecting ambiguous or malformed framing — socket timeouts, daemon handler threads and a bounded drain() over its tracked in-flight handlers) and SseWriter (one HTTP chunk per event, flushed; a : ping heartbeat from a companion thread; a failed write marks the stream broken exactly once and fires the response's on_disconnect). ApiError renders as the sanitized {"error": {...}} envelope; any other exception is a bare 500 and its traceback goes only to the --debug log. run_forever() serves on a worker thread with SIGINT/SIGTERM mapped to a clean shutdown(). It knows nothing about OpenAI or Ollama.
  22. artifacts.py — the artifact subsystem behind the serve API's files/artifacts endpoints and the file content parts: ArtifactStore (immutable snapshots behind opaque art_… ids; register() reserves quota in the index under the SessionStore lock pattern — RLock + flock — publishes with a temp file + os.replace, writes one authoritative manifest per artifact under meta/, and sweep()s TTL expiries, stale reservations and debris at startup and, rate-limited, on registration; every index/manifest path read back must resolve inside the store root) and ArtifactRef (the public record: id, media type, sanitized display filename, size, sha256, source, turn/session provenance, created_at and the relative url; TurnArtifacts is the turn-bound publisher tools receive through ToolContext.artifacts). The shared content layer lives here too: resolve_content_parts() maps text/image_url/file parts for both API surfaces (text inlining bounded by INLINE_TEXT_BYTES, TEXTUAL_MEDIA_TYPES as the deterministic text rule, binary parts described but never faked, missing ids a structured 404), charging every part/image/text byte to an optional InputBudget (InputLimits/input_limits, the aggregate serve_max_* caps: message/part counts, message and total text bytes, image counts and cumulative decoded image bytes), fetch_remote_media() is the one bounded http(s) fetch (redirects, timeouts, size cap) and require_vision() the one image capability check. It raises server.ApiError directly — it exists for the HTTP layer. Imports constants, helpers, server.
  23. fits.py — the context-fit jobs behind the native API's fit surface: FitService (a worker thread per job; queued → running → completed/failed/cancelled; per-session exclusivity, a global max_active_fits cap, cancel via the job's token, TTL sweeping of terminal jobs and an idempotent shutdown that cancels and joins) and FitJob/fit_body (the HTTP shape) plus FitBusy/TooManyFits/ FitsClosed. Jobs run one ctxfit.fit_context() and report progress through the request's on_progress; the optional session write is the API's on_success hook, so this module never touches the store.
  24. openai_api.py — the OpenAI-compatible /v1 surface (build_router() registers GET /v1/models, GET /v1/models/{id}, POST /v1/embeddings, POST /v1/chat/completions). Model turns only: parse_chat_request() validates the OpenAI schema (explicit 400s for unknown fields, n outside 1..8 or non-integer, logprobs, logit_bias, audio, non-text modalities, tool_choice: "required"), converts messages verbatim (assistant tool_calls, role: tool + tool_call_id→tool_name history, data-URI images) and ollama_payload() builds the /api/chat call; an n > 1 request emulates the fan-out as n sequential generations (indexed choices, summed usage, per-choice streaming indexes, capped at MAX_N = 8), and parallel_tool_calls: false is honored by truncating to the first returned call. parse_embeddings_request()/ embeddings_body() map POST /v1/embeddings onto /api/embed (string or string-array inputs, float/base64 encodings, dimensions forwarded, an embedding capability gate). Client tools pass through and never execute (the agent loop, tools registry and sessions are not reachable from this module). completion_body()/_stream_completion()/stream_chunk() shape the OpenAI response and SSE (role chunk, deltas, thinking as delta.reasoning_content, the tool calls as one indexed array chunk, finish reason, optional usage chunk, [DONE]); OpenAIApi keeps single-flight model-list/capability caches and builds one OllamaClient per request so a disconnecting client cancels only its own stream. The system extension ("auto" = built-in default, text = replace) is off unless asked. translate_error()/stream_backend_error() map upstream failures onto sanitized 404/502 envelopes with stable messages (raw backend detail goes to the --debug log).
  25. agent_api.py — the native agent endpoints (build_agent_api() constructs the one AgentApi; add_artifact_routes() registers the shared POST /v1/files and GET /v1/artifacts/* routes — kept even when serve_agent disables the agent surface — and add_agent_routes() registers POST /v1/agent/turns, GET /v1/agent/turns/{id} and .../events, POST .../cancel, POST /v1/agent/approvals/{id}, the /v1/sessions routes and the fit routes (POST /v1/agent/fit, POST /v1/agent/fits, GET /v1/agent/fits/{id}, POST /v1/agent/fits/{id}/cancel). parse_agent_turn() validates the turn body (new-session seed vs existing-session delta; settings.tools/max_rounds/approval/ system/parameters/cancel_on_disconnect). Each turn builds a headless Repl (its cancel_token and tool_ctx.cancel rewired to the turn's token) and runs AgentRuntime through TurnManager with the runtime's own tool execution, so the API approver and event sink apply to every round. The approver composes tools.policy_check (shared with the CLI), parks genuinely undecided calls in waiting_approval (PendingApproval + approval.required carrying its approval_id; the first decision wins, a timeout denies, cancellation resolves it as cancelled), and the serve tool policy is never auto. The events endpoint speaks the typed TurnEvent stream (id: <turn>:<seq>, ?after=/Last-Event-ID replay, stream.gap passthrough) and treats a disconnect as an unsubscribe unless cancel_on_disconnect; the status endpoint distinguishes 404 from 410 through TurnManager.expired(); session routes go through the store and refuse edits to a session with an active turn (409 session_busy, same as delete); serve_turn_timeout is a watchdog that cancels with reason timeout. The context warning/auto-compaction step runs headlessly at turn start through the runtime's on_started hook. Context control: PATCH/turn settings take num_ctx/gpu_layers (strictly validated; a placement change unloads the resident model) and a validated parameters merge (validate_settings_parameters: known Ollama options type/range checked, unknown names passed through bounded), settings.num_ctx: "max-gpu"|"max-cpu" estimates at turn start (estimate only) and rides the typed session.fit event plus result.fit, POST /v1/agent/fit serves the synchronous estimate with an optional apply, and POST /v1/agent/fits parks a probe job in fits.py. serve_fit gates off/estimate/probe; a fitting session is held by _fit_guard (409 session_busy with active_fit_id, checked alongside active turns by every session route and turn submit).
  26. cli.py — build_parser() (the full argparse surface, mirroring every ollama run flag), resolve_model/resolve_session (figuring out what model/session a given invocation means, including the -c/-r/ --session disambiguation in normalize_argv), ui_mode()/wants_tui() (which front end to start), build_serve_parser()/serve_main() (the ollamarun serve subcommand: upstream resolution, serve_settings() validation, banner, the combined OpenAI + agent router gated by serve_agent, and the ordered shutdown — refuse new work, cancel/join, drain handlers within serve_shutdown_timeout, then unload the tracked models unless --keep-loaded) and main() as the entry point (called by the top-level ollamarun script), which dispatches serve before the normal parser.

Model housekeeping (unload-before-switch, unload-on-exit, embedding models always resident) is cross-cutting logic that lives in the REPL commands (cmd_model, cmd_load, both in repl.py) and main()'s exit path (cli.py), coordinated through /api/ps lookups in OllamaClient — not a separate module. The model picker those commands (and a model-less ollamarun run) open is ordered by the session's model_sort, seeded from --sort and updated whenever a sort is chosen at the prompt.

Cross-module imports follow the numbering above (a module only imports from one earlier in the list, plus constants.py/helpers.py/events.py from anywhere) — keep new code on that side of the dependency graph rather than reaching "backwards" (e.g. don't import from repl.py inside renderer.py); use typing.TYPE_CHECKING for a backwards-pointing type hint only, the way renderer.py does for Session (defined later, in session.py).

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text:
• ollamarun — thin executable entry point (/bin/python3.10); adds its own directory to sys.path and calls into ollamarun_lib/.
  • ollamarun_lib/ — the implementation, one module per pipeline stage (math rendering, HTTP client, sessions, REPL, TUI, CLI, ...) — the module list above is the map.
  • ollamarun_lib/defs/ — the model-facing tool definitions and prompts.
  • test_ollamarun.py (and the serve half it imports) — the test suite; run with python3 test_ollamarun.py.
  • docs/ + mkdocs.yml — this documentation site.

CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md (mirror copies) carry the working guidance for agents editing this repo.

See Contributing for where to change what and the test suite.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
This is a personal project, but the internals are documented for anyone reading along. CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md (mirror copies) describe the module layout, the conventions (Python 3.10, rich, argparse in main()) and where to change what. There is no contribution process; issues are welcome, but the roadmap is whatever I am learning next — currently the web UI.

Run the tests with python3 test_ollamarun.py. The suite doubles as the compatibility contract for both API surfaces — it round-trips the official openai SDK and exercises a real ollamarun serve process against a stub backend — and --live adds a pass against a real Ollama server.

docs.title: Where to change what
docs.text:
• New tool: add defs/tools/NAME.json (description, JSON schema, safety flags, optional requires/aliases, handler name), the handler function and its HANDLERS entry in tools.py, and a row in the README tool table. Registration is data-driven — default_registry() picks the file up automatically, and read_only/always_safe feed approval_decision().
  • New slash command: one cmd_NAME(repl, argument) function in repl.py, wired into COMMAND_INFO/COMMAND_HANDLERS; complete the build_parser() epilog and the README command table when it is notable.
  • New config key: add it to DEFAULT_CONFIG in constants.py and to the README's selected-keys list; user config merges over the defaults.
  • New inspection output (--list-style): build it into a cli_* function and route through emit() (emit.py), never a hand-rolled table.
  • New example client: examples/ holds the runnable reference clients (the official-SDK one and the native-agent one); they double as the test_examples regression against the fake stack and are covered by the pyflakes gate, so keep them clean, runnable and mirrored in the README's Example clients section.
  • New interactive prompt/hook: extend the Ui protocol and ConsoleUi in ui.py, then implement it in TuiUi (tui.py) — nothing below the repl.py layer may know which front end is running. Set interactive on an implementation that can actually ask; the approval gate reads it.
  • New runtime event: add the type to events.py, emit it from runtime.py, and teach the consumers (Repl's event printer, HeadlessRenderer, the future HTTP layer) — the event stream is the contract between the runtime and every front end.
  • New /v1 endpoint: register it in openai_api.build_router() (OpenAI-compatible surface) or the right native group — agent_api.add_agent_routes() (turns/sessions/fits) or add_artifact_routes() (shared files/artifacts), and keep transport concerns in server.py (body caps, SSE framing, error envelopes); handlers raise ApiError for structured errors and return a Response or StreamResponse. The agent layer reuses turns.py's manager plus a headless Repl, never the OpenAI mapping.
  • New model-facing text: tool wording in defs/tools/*.json, prompt text in defs/prompts/; never hardcode it in Python.
  • Streaming/rendering UX: renderer.py (the TUI consumes the same frames through StreamSink), and ui.py's StatusSnapshot/format_status() when it shows up in the status bar.
  • New docs page: place it under its surface — docs/cli/, docs/api/, docs/tui/, docs/web-ui/ — or the global docs/getting-started// docs/config/; register it in mkdocs.yml's nav and assemble it from existing sources with --8<-- snippet includes (README.md, a marked AGENTS.md section, plans/) rather than copying text. Command collections stay on one reference page. Verify with mkdocs build --strict.

docs.title: Testing notes
docs.text: The suite is two files: test_ollamarun.py (the shared harness, CLI, renderer and tool tests) and test_ollamarun_serve.py (everything runtime/turns/serve/agent/artifact/fit); the canonical command python3 test_ollamarun.py imports and runs both. Tests are table-driven: some sections are a CASES-style list of (name, input, predicate) tuples run through a small harness, others are a test_*() -> int function that prints PASS/FAIL lines and returns a failure count, mirroring the pattern documented in ~/bin/AGENTS.md (test_modelbenchmark.py is the canonical example there); all test_* functions are summed in the if __name__ == "__main__": block at the bottom. The math-rendering tests (MATH_CASES) are the largest block and the most likely place a change to the layout engine (mathrender.py) will need new coverage. OllamaClient is tested against a fake requests.Session (_FakeSession/_FakeResponse) rather than a real HTTP mock library; REPL/CLI-level tests use _FakeClient (a lighter double with the handful of methods those layers actually call) instead. Console output assertions that capture the shared console singleton (with orun.console.capture() as cap:) should go through the _plain() helper before substring-matching, since rich's automatic number/keyword highlighting can split a literal substring across ANSI color codes. The Phase 1/1b runtime tests (test_runtime_events, test_headless_renderer, test_session_store_lock, test_session_store_cross_process_lock, test_ui_interactive, test_tool_cancellation, test_cancellation_coverage, test_file_mention_inlining, test_tool_support_warning, test_quiet_tools_live, test_approval_event_contract, test_python310_syntax, test_turn_result_mapping) cover the AgentRuntime event stream, the terminal-free turn path, the in-process/cross-process store locks, turn cancellation (including the ssh/chem/tts/trash coverage), @file inlining, the approval event contract and the 3.10 syntax guard. The audit guards (test_runtime_event_contract, test_approval_runtime_contract, test_unattended_turn_denial, test_cancel_reaches_production_tools, test_quiet_tools_real_turn, test_session_store_process_gate, test_session_store_same_session_writers, test_session_store_without_fcntl, test_cancellation_destructive_guard) pin the event vocabulary/serialization and terminal-event contract, the approval order with its interrupt/stopped paths, the cancel token actually reaching a production turn's tool, the store flock gating another process, and the destructive-tool refusal after a stop. The Phase 2 tests (test_turn_event_envelope, test_turn_manager_lifecycle, test_turn_manager_synthesized_terminal, test_turn_buffer_truncation, test_turn_expired, test_turn_manager_session_busy, test_turn_manager_max_active, test_turn_manager_cancel, test_turn_subscriber_overflow, test_turn_manager_shutdown, test_turn_manager_context, test_turn_manager_headless_turn) cover envelopes, lifecycle, replay/gap/truncation, session exclusivity, the active cap, cancellation, overflow and shutdown. The Phase 3 serve tests (test_openai_mapping, test_embeddings_api, test_serve_http, test_serve_disconnect, test_serve_sockets, test_serve_cache_concurrency, test_serve_cli, test_openai_sdk) pin request validation and message/tool mapping (strict types, exact error envelopes), the embeddings schema and gates, n > 1 and parallel_tool_calls behavior, the live HTTP surface over a fake backend (models, non-stream and SSE chat, tool calls, the vision gate, body and image caps), client-disconnect cancellation with stream isolation, the wired request timeout (stalled body 408, streams outliving it), single-flight caches, the serve parser, config defaults and main() dispatch, and the official OpenAI SDK round-trip including negative and mid-stream-failure paths (a required gate: it fails when the package is missing and prints the SDK version it exercised). The Phase 6 hardening tests (test_serve_config_matrix, test_chunked_bodies, test_input_limits, test_native_parameters, test_workspace_jail, test_artifact_root_containment, test_serve_model_gate, test_serve_agent_switch, test_serve_shutdown, test_serve_unload_on_exit) pin the validated serve matrix and its transport wiring, chunked decoding, the aggregate resolved-input budget, native option validation, the workspace jail, artifact-root containment, the model allowlist, the serve_agent route groups, the shutdown order and the tracked unload. test_serve_process spawns the real ollamarun serve binary against a stub upstream (banner-discovered address, a completion, a SIGTERM mid-stream drain, a clean exit, the tracked unload), test_turn_mode_isolation pins the model-turn-vs-agent-turn contrast, test_examples runs both reference clients against the fake stack, and test_pyflakes_clean is the lint gate (it covers ollamarun_lib/, the examples/ clients, the entry script and both test files). python3 test_ollamarun.py --live additionally runs a real-backend smoke test (models, completion with usage, streaming, embeddings — OLLAMARUN_TEST_EMBED_MODEL overrides the first embedding-capable pick — and one full agent turn; tool round-trip with OLLAMARUN_TEST_MODEL set). The Phase 4 agent tests (test_agent_turn_lifecycle, test_agent_turn_controls, test_agent_approvals, test_agent_approval_edge, test_agent_policy_mode, test_agent_disconnect_policy, test_agent_turn_timeout, test_agent_sessions_api, test_agent_turn_validation, test_agent_turn_expiry, test_agent_context_warning) pin the full-turn path (202/status/events/session persistence), session-busy 409 with the active id and the global-cap 429, approval parking with run/remember/deny and duplicate rejection, approval timeout, cancellation and shutdown while waiting, policy-mode allow/deny, disconnect vs cancel_on_disconnect, the wall-clock turn timeout, the session CRUD routes, the turn-schema malformed matrix, 404/410 turn status and the headless context warning/compaction. The Phase 5 artifact tests (test_artifact_store, test_artifact_quota_and_ttl, test_tool_artifact_registration, test_artifact_events, test_artifact_session_persistence, test_artifact_content_parts, test_artifact_remote_fetch, test_artifact_upload_api, test_artifact_fetch_api, test_serve_approval_timeout_zero) pin the store (ids, hashes, immutability, traversal-shaped ids, sanitized names, concurrent quota reservations, TTL/reconciliation sweeps), tool publication (file tools' destinations, publish_artifact jailing and gating, note-not-failure), the artifact.created ordering and persistence, the shared content resolver (inlining, binary notes, 404s, remote-fetch rules against a local stub server) and the HTTP endpoints (201 refs, strict validation, 413/507, download headers, 404 and the no-store 503). The Phase 10 context-control tests (test_ctxfit_outcome, test_ctxfit_cancel_progress, test_fit_service, test_session_context_fields, test_fit_estimate_api, test_fit_job_api, test_turn_start_fit) pin the structured fit_context() outcome and its data-shaped failures, cancellation at estimate/probe checkpoints and progress stages, the fit service (lifecycle, caps, per-session exclusivity, TTL, apply hook, shutdown), the first-class num_ctx/gpu_layers fields (strict validation, unload parity, persistence), the estimate endpoint matrix and policy gates, the async job API (202 + warnings, status/progress, cancel, apply, 404/409/429) and the turn-start estimate (session.fit, result.fit, persistence, the no-change failure path). Fit tests inject the machine (MachineGpu) and read-only RAM probes, so they need no GPU.

docs.title: Docs site
docs.text:
The site is MkDocs + Material: mkdocs.yml is the whole configuration and docs/ holds one page per feature, grouped by surface — cli/, api/, tui/, web-ui/ — with global material in getting-started/, config/, project/, development/ and design/. Collections that are one feature (the slash commands, the tools) get a single reference page with a section per item.

Two kinds of pages:

  • Feature pages mirror the README's material page by page — the README is the GitHub front page, the site is the browsable version — so a behavior change updates both.
  • A few pages are snippet includes of the repository's own files, so they cannot drift from their sources:
Page Source development/architecture.md the marked architecture section of AGENTS.md development/contributing.md the marked where-to-change and testing sections of AGENTS.md design/api-layer.md the marked api-layer section of ollamarunAPILayerPlan.md

Install the tooling (mkdocs-material pulls in mkdocs and pymdown-extensions; on a PEP 668 box add --break-system-packages, which still only touches the user site) and build:

$ pip install --user mkdocs-material
$ mkdocs serve            # live preview on http://127.0.0.1:8000
$ mkdocs build --strict   # warnings fail the build; run before deploying

Deploying is mkdocs gh-deploy: it builds the site and pushes the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves at https://vinibretas.github.io/ollamarun/.

To add a page, put it under its surface (or getting-started//config/ for global material), register it in mkdocs.yml's nav, and prefer an include over copying text. Feature pages created as stubs carry a single *This page is not written yet.* line; replace it when the page is written.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: ollamarun is a single executable plus one Python package — there is no build step and nothing to compile. It runs anywhere Linux does, as long as a Python 3.10+ and a reachable Ollama server are around.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: What Why Linux The harness leans on Linux behavior: /proc/meminfo for the RAM fits, nvidia-smi for GPU probes, trash-put for deletes, PTYs for the inline REPL. Python 3.10+ The entry script pins /bin/python3.10; the code targets 3.10 and does not use newer stdlib without guards. A reachable Ollama server All inference, model listing and model management go to Ollama over its HTTP API. Default 127.0.0.1:11434; see pointing at Ollama below.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
Clone the repository somewhere it can live permanently:

$ git clone https://github.com/vinibretas/ollamarun.git
$ cd ollamarun

The ollamarun file at the root is the whole entry point: it adds its own directory to sys.path and calls into ollamarun_lib/, so the two must stay together. If the checkout already sits on your PATH (this project is also a git submodule of my personal ~/bin), the bare ollamarun command resolves straight to it.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
$ pip install --user rich requests prompt_toolkit

Those three are the required runtime dependencies: rich for the rendering, requests for the HTTP API and prompt_toolkit for the inline REPL. On a PEP 668 "externally managed" distribution, add --break-system-packages (it still only touches your user site) or use a virtualenv.

Everything else is optional and degrades gracefully:

Extra Enables Without it pylatexenc The best-quality LaTeX → Unicode conversion A smaller built-in macro table does the conversion; nothing crashes. textual The deprecated --ui tui front end --ui tui warns and falls back to the inline REPL. ddgs The web_search tool The tool is not offered to the model. pypdf PDF text extraction for fetch_url Falls back to pdftotext when it is installed. pyperclip /copy writes to the clipboard /copy reports that pyperclip is missing.

A few tools are wired to external commands and appear only where those resolve: tts-remote (the speak/list_voices tools), chemInventoryAPI (the read-only chem_* lookups), plus system tools the harness calls when present — trash-put (deletes), pdftotext (PDFs), nvidia-smi (GPU probes) and tailscale (--remote).

To run the test suite you additionally need the official SDK and the linter:

$ pip install --user openai pyflakes
$ python3 test_ollamarun.py

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
$ ./ollamarun --version
ollamarun 2.0

./ollamarun --help prints the full flag surface (the same reference this site keeps in Usage and flags) and ./ollamarun serve --help covers the API server.

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
Nothing needs configuring up front. The first run creates the config file from the built-in defaults, so a plain one-shot is enough to prove everything works:

$ ollamarun --no-tools llama3.2:3b "Say hello in one short sentence."
llama3.2:3b ›
Hello.

(That transcript is verbatim from a real run; llama3.2:3b happens to answer in one or two words. Without --no-tools it may also call the shell — that is the tool harness doing its job.)

  • Config: ~/etc/config_files/ollamarun.json — created on first run; see Config file for every key.
  • Sessions: one JSON file plus an index under ~/etc/data/ollamarun/ — see Storage.
  • Logs: ~/etc/logs/ollamarun.log receives the debug log when --debug is set.

If the model is not installed on the target machine, the run does not fail silently: it prints the machine's free disk space and offers to pull the model (per-layer progress included). --pull skips the question, declining opens the model picker, and /pull does the same from inside the REPL.

docs.title: Pointing at Ollama
docs.text:
In precedence order, the upstream server comes from:

  1. --host HOST[:PORT] on the command line.
  2. --remote NAME for a tailnet machine — see Remote inference.
  3. The OLLAMA_HOST environment variable.
  4. The host config key.
  5. The default, 127.0.0.1:11434.

ollamarun serve has its own, separate --host/--remote for the upstream; the API listener is chosen with --bind/--port — see API overview.

docs.title: Running it without the checkout (optional)
docs.text:
The executable is self-contained with its package next to it, so putting the checkout on PATH is enough:

$ export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/code/ollamarun"    # then: ollamarun ...

The shebang /bin/python3.10 matters only for the bare ./ollamarun form; if that interpreter lives elsewhere, call it explicitly with any 3.10+ Python instead:

$ python3 /path/to/ollamarun --version

That works because the entry script re-adds its own directory to sys.path before importing the package.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Needs Linux, Python 3.10+ and a reachable Ollama server — everything else is covered in Installation. This page is the shortest path from zero to a working run, a REPL and the API layer; every command below was executed as shown.

docs.title: One-shot
docs.text:
$ ollamarun --no-tools llama3.2:3b "Say hello in one short sentence."
llama3.2:3b ›
Hello.

With a PROMPT argument the run is a single generation that exits when the answer is done. Drop the prompt and it is an interactive session instead:

$ ollamarun llama3.2:3b              # the inline REPL
$ ollamarun                          # model picker first, then the REPL

Piped stdin works as the prompt too, so it slots into scripts:

$ printf 'What is 2+2? Answer with the number only.\n' | ollamarun --no-tools llama3.2:3b
llama3.2:3b ›
4

Useful one-shot switches: --raw writes only the answer text, --json writes the final Ollama response payload (with usage and timings), --no-save keeps the run out of the session store, and -y removes tool-approval prompts when the model is allowed to act on its own. The full surface is in Usage and flags.

docs.title: The REPL
docs.text:
A model-less run opens the picker; a run with a model goes straight to the inline prompt:

╭─ ollamarun ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ model   llama3.2:3b                                                  │
│ session 20261018-105614-b08e · new session                           │
│ host    http://127.0.0.1:11434                                       │
│ render  markdown · thinking collapsed · 95 local models              │
│ /help for commands · Ctrl+D to exit · Ctrl+T thinking                │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
llama3.2:3b ›

Everything interactive lives behind slash commands — /model, /params, /tools, /undo, /branch, /export, /bye — and a @path mention inlines a file into the next prompt. Start with The REPL, Slash commands and @file mentions.

Sessions persist as you go: leave the REPL and come back with -c (the most recent session) or --session NAME; browse everything with --list. See Sessions.

docs.title: The API layer
docs.text:
ollamarun serve faces both the OpenAI API and the native agent API over one listener. Start it, then talk to it with any OpenAI client or curl:

$ ollamarun serve --port 0 --keep-loaded
ollamarun serve · 2.0 · OpenAI-compatible + agent API
  listening http://0.0.0.0:44611 (all interfaces)
  upstream  http://127.0.0.1:11434
  workspace /home/you/code/ollamarun
  models /v1/models · chat /v1/chat/completions · agent turns /v1/agent/turns ·
sessions /v1/sessions
trusted-network-only: no authentication — never expose this port to the internet
Ctrl-C stops the server (active turns are cancelled; loaded models are kept)

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:44611/v1/chat/completions \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"model": "llama3.2:3b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with exactly: pong"}]}'

{
  "id": "chatcmpl-44c986f679d84aa498b3ed86",
  "object": "chat.completion",
  "created": 1792331897,
  "model": "llama3.2:3b",
  "choices": [
    {
      "index": 0,
      "message": {"role": "assistant", "content": "pong"},
      "finish_reason": "stop"
    }
  ],
  "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 30, "completion_tokens": 2, "total_tokens": 32}
}

Two runnable reference clients double as integration checks — the official openai SDK one and a native agent-flow one:

$ python3 examples/openai_client.py --model llama3.2:3b
$ python3 examples/agent_client.py --prompt "List the files in /tmp"
  • API overview — both surfaces, the listener and the lifecycle.
  • Example clients — what each client exercises.
  • OpenAI API and Agent API — the full reference.

Trusted-network-only

The service has no authentication and the bind address is its only boundary. Keep it on the LAN/tailnet; never expose the port to the public internet.

docs.title: Acknowledgements
docs.text:
This project exists mostly because of other people's work:

  • Ollama — the local server every request goes through. The whole harness is an unaffiliated wrapper around its HTTP API, and a very happy user of it.
  • The OpenAI API — the ollamarun serve /v1 surface reimplements OpenAI's HTTP schema (chat completions, embeddings, SSE streaming, tool calls) so unmodified OpenAI clients work against local models. "OpenAI-compatible" is descriptive only — no affiliation with, or endorsement by, OpenAI is implied.
  • llama.cpp — its KV-cache geometry and fit arithmetic are what the context/placement fitting is modelled on, and it performs the actual inference behind Ollama.
  • The Python ecosystem — rich (rendering, tables, progress), prompt_toolkit (the inline REPL), Textual (the TUI), pylatexenc (inline-math fallback), ddgs (web search), pypdf (PDF text extraction), pyperclip (clipboard) and requests (HTTP) — plus the official openai SDK, which the test suite round-trips as the compatibility contract.
  • The system tools it leans on — Tailscale (--remote), trash-cli (trash-put deletes), poppler (pdftotext) and NVIDIA's nvidia-smi (GPU probes).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ollamarun began as a nicer ollama run: streamed markdown, 2D Unicode math, sessions that actually persist. It has since grown into a full harness — an approval-gated tool loop, two front ends, remote inference, context/GPU placement fitting, and an HTTP API layer (ollamarun serve) that speaks both the OpenAI API and its own native agent API.

This is not a product. It is a one-person workbench for learning how local LLM stacks fit together, and how much of a real agent harness you can build around one. Every ollama run flag (ollama 0.34) is accepted and extended, so it still doubles as a drop-in replacement for the CLI it started as.

docs.title: What I'm using it to learn
docs.text:
• Local LLM orchestration — talking to Ollama over raw HTTP, streaming responses by hand, model lifecycle (/api/ps, load/unload), GPU placement.
  • Harness engineering — the unglamorous middle of agents: tool schemas, approvals that do not get in the way, cancellation, output truncation, and keeping a model on the rails across multi-round tool loops.
  • API compatibility and support — making unmodified OpenAI clients work against local models (strict validation, SSE, embeddings, emulated n > 1), plus a native agent API (turns, events, parked approvals, sessions, fits) for clients that want the whole loop.
  • Terminal UX — live markdown re-rendering, a self-contained LaTeX → 2D Unicode math layout engine, a collapsible thinking panel, tok/s + context footers.
  • Systems math — sizing context windows from GGUF metadata and KV-cache geometry, VRAM budgets, and calibrating estimates with measured probes.
  • Data-driven prompting — tool definitions and system prompts as editable files, not Python strings.

docs.title: The path so far
docs.text:
1. ollama run, but nicer — richer rendering, 2D math, persistent sessions, slash commands.
  2. Tools and approvals — Ollama function calling with a read-only allowlist, numbered approval prompts with remembered rules, and sessions that keep the whole tool loop.
  3. A real terminal app — a Textual TUI, remote inference over Tailscale, GPU/context fitting, image input, artifacts.
  4. An API layer — ollamarun serve: an OpenAI-compatible /v1 surface plus a native agent API for full turns, with reference clients and a compatibility test suite.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Early, single-developer and moving. Built against one Linux box and a small Tailscale fleet; Python 3.10; a few tools are wired to my own side projects and degrade gracefully when those are absent. Rough edges are part of the deal — expect the structure to keep changing as the learning continues.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
The main thing on the roadmap is a web interface on top of ollamarun serve as its backend. The native agent API already has the shape a browser client needs — submit a turn, follow its event stream, answer parked approvals, manage sessions and files — because that is the same loop the terminal drives.

docs.title: Textual TUI (deprecated)
docs.text:
Deprecated. The Textual front end still works, but it is not the future: it talks to the runtime in-process, and it will be rewritten as a pure client of the ollamarun serve API — the same direction as the planned web UI. The inline REPL is the supported front end meanwhile.

--ui tui (config "ui": "tui", or --ui auto to use it when the optional textual package is installed) separates the interactive session into panes: the transcript up top, a rule, a status bar (spinner + state, model and remote, thinking/tools/render modes, context tokens and %, live tok/s, queued count, key hints) and an input box that stays available while the model works.

  • Type while it works. Enter queues the message and it is handed to the model at the next sub-task boundary — right after a tool result, or in a follow-up round when an answer finishes streaming — so the model continues with the new information instead of dropping what it was doing. Commands that only read state or change display knobs run immediately; the rest queue and run once the turn ends, in order (/queue shows/edits the list).
  • Ctrl+B sends what is typed right now: it cuts a streaming answer short but never kills a tool that is already running (the command keeps running and the model gets its result with your message in the next round).
  • Esc Esc stops the turn (the first Esc arms it). The partial answer is kept as a cancelled message and anything queued then runs as the next turn.
  • Ctrl+T thinking, Ctrl+G $EDITOR, Ctrl+L clear the transcript, Ctrl+Q quit (a second press when busy or with queued items), Tab completion and Up/Down history shared with the inline REPL. Tool approvals ask in a modal (y/a/n/A).

OLLAMARUN_TUI_FULLSCREEN=1 runs the app on the alternate screen (the transcript disappears on exit instead of staying in the terminal), and OLLAMA_TUI_DISABLE keeps --ui tui on the inline REPL. The inline REPL is also the fallback whenever Textual is missing or the output is not a terminal.
